records.greek: Τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ ἔρχεται πρωῒ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, καὶ βλέπει τὸν λίθον ἠρμένον ἐκ τοῦ μνημείου.
records.gloss: On the now first [day] of the sabbaths Mary the Magdalene comes early, darkness still being, to the tomb, and sees the stone having been taken away from the tomb.

L.1: Now on the first [day] of the week Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and sees the stone taken away from the tomb.

R.1: It was the first day of the week, very early, and it was still dark. Mary Magdalene made her way to the tomb, and she saw that the stone had been moved away from it.

decisions.choice: the first of the sabbaths: the first day of the week, the day after the Sabbath
decisions.reason: The plural of the word for Sabbath was also used for the week, and "the first" means its first day. It is the day we call Sunday. Jesus had been buried in haste on the Friday, the day of Preparation, before the Sabbath began (19:31, 42), and nothing could be done on the Sabbath itself. Mary comes as soon as the Sabbath is over. The same phrase opens the evening scene in verse 19.

decisions.choice: Mary Magdalene: Mary from Magdala
decisions.reason: Magdala was a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. John has already named her among the women standing near the cross (19:25). Luke says that she had followed Jesus from Galilee after he set her free from seven demons (Luke 8:2). Nothing in the Gospels makes her the sinful woman of Luke 7:36-50.

decisions.choice: early, while it was still dark: before dawn
decisions.reason: πρωῒ is the last part of the night, before sunrise (Mark 13:35 uses it for the last watch). John adds that it was still dark. The other Gospels speak of the women coming as the sun rose (Mark 16:2); the details fit a walk that began in the dark and ended at first light.

decisions.choice: sees the stone taken away: she sees that it has been moved, not who moved it
alternatives: sees the stone being taken away
decisions.reason: The participle is passive and in the perfect: the stone has been lifted away and is no longer in place. Mary sees the result and draws her own conclusion in verse 2. A stone closed the opening of the tomb, as at Lazarus's tomb (11:38-39).

decisions.choice: comes, sees (L); came, found (B); made her way, saw (R)
decisions.reason: John tells much of this passage in the present tense, the historic present: she "comes" and "sees", she "runs", Peter "comes" and "sees", Jesus "says". It is a lively way of telling a story. Literal keeps the present so that readers see the Greek form; Balanced and Readable use the past, which is the normal tense for telling a story in English. This decision covers every historic present in 20:1-18.

decisions.choice: the first day of the week
decisions.reason: Every level keeps John's way of naming the day (meaning decision m1) rather than "Sunday", so that readers can see the link with verse 19.

records.heading: The empty tomb

records.greek: τρέχει οὖν καὶ ἔρχεται πρὸς Σίμωνα Πέτρον καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἄλλον μαθητὴν ὃν ἐφίλει ὁ Ἰησοῦς, καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἦραν τὸν κύριον ἐκ τοῦ μνημείου, καὶ οὐκ οἴδαμεν ποῦ ἔθηκαν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Runs therefore and comes to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom was loving the Jesus, and says to them, "They took the Lord out of the tomb, and not we know where they laid him."

L.2: So she runs and comes to Simon Peter and to the other disciple, whom Jesus loved, and says to them, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid Him."

R.2: So she ran to Simon Peter, and to the other disciple too, the one whom Jesus loved. She told them, "Someone has taken the Lord away from the tomb! We do not know where they have put Him."

decisions.choice: whom Jesus loved: the disciple of 13:23 and 19:26, here with the other verb for love
decisions.reason: Elsewhere John speaks of the disciple whom Jesus loved with the other common verb for love (13:23; 19:26; 21:7, 20); only here does he use ἐφίλει for this disciple. John uses both verbs for Jesus's love for Lazarus (11:3, 5) and for the Father's love for the Son (3:35; 5:20), so the change does not point to a different kind of love. The disciple is not named.

decisions.choice: they have taken: someone, not named
alternatives: the Jewish authorities have taken him
decisions.reason: The plural verb has no subject; it means that someone has done it. Mary does not say who. She assumes that the body has been moved, whether by grave robbers or by those in charge of the tomb, and she does not yet think of resurrection.

decisions.choice: we do not know: a hint that Mary was not alone
alternatives: we: Mary and the disciples together
we: a way of speaking, meaning only Mary
decisions.reason: Only Mary is named in verse 1, but she says "we". The other Gospels say that other women came to the tomb with her (Matthew 28:1; Mark 16:1; Luke 24:10), and the plural may reflect that. It may also be a way of speaking for the disciples as a group. In verse 13 she says "I do not know".

decisions.choice: the Lord: Jesus, called by the title his followers gave him
alternatives: the master (a title of respect only)
decisions.reason: Mary speaks as a disciple: she calls Jesus "the Lord" even when she thinks only of his body. The narrator uses the same title once Jesus is risen (20:20), and Mary's report in verse 18 is "I have seen the Lord".

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: Mary speaks of Jesus's body, but she means Jesus himself, so the pronoun takes the deity_pronoun setting like every pronoun for him.

decisions.choice: Someone has taken
decisions.reason: Readable shows that the subject of "they have taken" is not named (meaning decision m2); the following "they" then refers back to that someone.

records.greek: ἐξῆλθεν οὖν ὁ Πέτρος καὶ ὁ ἄλλος μαθητής, καὶ ἤρχοντο εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον.
records.gloss: Went out therefore the Peter and the other disciple, and were coming to the tomb.

L.3: So Peter and the other disciple went out, and they were going to the tomb.

R.3: So Peter and the other disciple left and headed for the tomb.

decisions.choice: went out: a singular verb with two subjects, Peter named first
decisions.reason: The first verb is singular, as Greek often has when it comes before two subjects; Peter is named first, as the one who sets out. The second verb is plural and in the imperfect: the two were on their way to the tomb. Verse 4 then tells how they ran.

decisions.choice: were coming to the tomb: were going there
decisions.reason: The verb means to come or to go, depending on the point of view. Told from the tomb, where Mary had been, they were "coming" to it; in plain terms they were on their way there.

decisions.choice: set out and made their way (B); left and headed for (R)
decisions.reason: Natural phrases for the start of the journey and the journey under way (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἔτρεχον δὲ οἱ δύο ὁμοῦ· καὶ ὁ ἄλλος μαθητὴς προέδραμεν τάχιον τοῦ Πέτρου καὶ ἦλθεν πρῶτος εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, καὶ παρακύψας βλέπει κείμενα τὰ ὀθόνια, οὐ μέντοι εἰσῆλθεν.
records.gloss: Were running now the two together; and the other disciple ran ahead more quickly [than] the Peter and came first to the tomb, \v 5 and having stooped sees lying the linen cloths, not however he went in.

L.4: And the two were running together; and the other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and came to the tomb first,
L.5: and stooping down he sees the linen cloths lying [there]; yet he did not go in.

R.4: Both of them were running, but the other disciple ran faster than Peter and got to the tomb first.
R.5: He bent down and looked inside. He saw the linen cloths lying in the tomb, but he did not go in.

decisions.choice: the linen cloths: the burial wrappings Joseph and Nicodemus had put on the body
decisions.reason: ὀθόνια is the word used in 19:40, where Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bound Jesus's body in linen cloths with the spices. It is a different word from the strips that bound Lazarus's hands and feet (11:44). Whether these were long strips or larger pieces of linen, the word does not say.

decisions.choice: stooping down: bending to look in through a low opening
decisions.reason: The verb means to bend over in order to look into something. The openings of rock tombs were often low, so a person had to stoop to see inside. Mary does the same in verse 11.

decisions.choice: lying ... yet he did not go in: what he saw, and that he stopped there
decisions.reason: The cloths were "lying", that is, still in the tomb where the body had been. John notes that this disciple came first but did not go in, and does not say why. Verse 8 takes up the point when he does go in.

decisions.choice: Bending down to look in (B); bent down and looked inside (R)
decisions.reason: The verb itself means bending in order to look (meaning decision m2), so Balanced and Readable say so.

decisions.choice: linen cloths
decisions.reason: Every level uses the same words as in 19:40 for the same burial wrappings, and keeps them apart from the "strips of cloth" of 11:44, which is another word.

records.greek: ἔρχεται οὖν καὶ Σίμων Πέτρος ἀκολουθῶν αὐτῷ, καὶ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον· καὶ θεωρεῖ τὰ ὀθόνια κείμενα, καὶ τὸ σουδάριον, ὃ ἦν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ, οὐ μετὰ τῶν ὀθονίων κείμενον ἀλλὰ χωρὶς ἐντετυλιγμένον εἰς ἕνα τόπον·
records.gloss: Comes therefore also Simon Peter following him, and went into the tomb; and sees the linen cloths lying, \v 7 and the face cloth, which was upon the head of him, not with the linen cloths lying but apart having been rolled up into one place;

L.6: Then Simon Peter also comes, following him, and went into the tomb; and he sees the linen cloths lying [there],
L.7: and the face cloth, which had been on His head, not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up apart in one place.

R.6: Simon Peter came up behind him and went right into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there.
R.7: He also saw the cloth that had been around Jesus's head. It was not with the linen cloths. It was rolled up and lying by itself.

decisions.choice: the face cloth: a smaller cloth for the head and face
decisions.reason: σουδάριον is the cloth that was tied around Lazarus's face (11:44). Here it had been on Jesus's head. Lazarus came out of his tomb still bound in his wrappings and had to be set free; Jesus has left his behind.

decisions.choice: rolled up apart in one place: folded or rolled together, lying by itself
alternatives: still in the shape in which it had wrapped the head
decisions.reason: ἐντετυλιγμένον means wrapped, rolled or folded up. The form is passive and perfect: the cloth lay rolled up. John does not say who rolled it. "Into one place" means in a place on its own, apart from the linen cloths.

decisions.choice: the order of the grave clothes: a detail that tells against a hurried theft
alternatives: a detail with no further point
decisions.reason: John describes the cloths with care, but he does not explain them. Their state does not fit Mary's fear that the body had been carried off (verse 2): those who move or steal a body do not first unwrap it and leave the cloths behind in order. The detail prepares for what the other disciple sees and believes in verse 8.

decisions.choice: comes ... went in: Peter arrives second but goes in first
decisions.reason: John moves between the present ("comes", "sees") and the past ("went in"); see the historic present at 20:1. Peter follows the other disciple, but he goes straight into the tomb.

decisions.choice: Jesus's head
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, since "his head" straight after "him" (the other disciple) could be misread.

decisions.choice: face cloth (L, B); the cloth that had been around Jesus's head (R)
decisions.reason: "Face cloth" names the same cloth as at Lazarus's tomb (11:44, "a cloth tied around his face"); Readable describes it by where it had been.

records.greek: τότε οὖν εἰσῆλθεν καὶ ὁ ἄλλος μαθητὴς ὁ ἐλθὼν πρῶτος εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, καὶ εἶδεν καὶ ἐπίστευσεν·
records.gloss: Then therefore went in also the other disciple, the [one] having come first to the tomb, and he saw and believed;

L.8: Then the other disciple also, the one who had come to the tomb first, went in, and he saw and believed.

R.8: Then the other disciple went in too, the one who had reached the tomb first. He saw, and he believed.

decisions.choice: believed: he came to believe that Jesus had risen
alternatives: he believed Mary's report that the body had been taken
decisions.reason: John does not say what he believed. The most natural sense is that what he saw in the tomb brought him to believe that Jesus had been raised. Verse 9 explains why it took seeing: they did not yet understand from the Scriptures that he must rise. Some take the verb to mean only that he now believed Mary's report that the body was gone, but John uses the verb for full belief, and he would hardly say "he saw and believed" of that alone. This disciple believes without yet seeing Jesus himself; compare 20:29.

decisions.choice: saw: he saw the empty tomb and the cloths
alternatives: a growing depth of sight from one verb to the next
decisions.reason: John uses three verbs for seeing in these verses: βλέπει (verse 5), θεωρεῖ (verse 6) and εἶδεν (here). In John these verbs overlap a great deal, and the change need not mark steps of deeper insight. What matters is that this time seeing leads to believing.

decisions.choice: the one who had come first: he reached the tomb first but went in second
decisions.reason: John repeats that this disciple arrived first (verse 4). The order is told plainly; the text draws no contest between the two disciples from it.

decisions.choice: he saw and believed
alternatives: he saw and believed that Jesus had risen
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the two verbs without an object, as John does, so that what he believed stays as open as in the original (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: οὐδέπω γὰρ ᾔδεισαν τὴν γραφὴν ὅτι δεῖ αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῆναι.
records.gloss: Not yet for they knew the scripture, that it is necessary him from [the] dead to rise.

L.9: For they did not yet know the Scripture, that He must rise from [the] dead.

R.9: Until then they had not understood that the Scriptures said He had to rise from the dead.

decisions.choice: knew: understood
decisions.reason: They knew the Scriptures as words; what they did not yet know was their meaning. John says the same of the disciples' understanding after the resurrection at 2:22 and 12:16. The "they" are the two disciples, and the verse explains why it was seeing, not the Scriptures, that brought the other disciple to believe.

decisions.choice: the Scripture: John names no passage
decisions.reason: The singular may point to one passage or speak of Scripture as a whole. The first Christians found the resurrection foretold in Psalm 16:10 (Acts 2:24-32; 13:35) and spoke of Christ being raised "according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:4; Luke 24:25-27, 44-46). John does not say which text he has in mind.

decisions.choice: must: the necessity of God's plan
decisions.reason: δεῖ is the word John uses for what has to happen by God's will: the Son of Man "must" be lifted up (3:14; 12:34). The rising from the dead was part of that plan, not an accident.

decisions.choice: understand (B); had not understood (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "understand" for the sense of the verb here (meaning decision m1); Literal keeps "know".

decisions.choice: the Scriptures said
decisions.reason: Readable uses the plural, the common way of speaking of the whole of Scripture, since John names no one passage (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ἀπῆλθον οὖν πάλιν πρὸς αὑτοὺς οἱ μαθηταί.
records.gloss: Went away therefore again to themselves the disciples.

L.10: So the disciples went away again to their own [places].

R.10: Then the two disciples went back to where they were staying.

decisions.choice: to themselves: to their own lodgings
decisions.reason: The phrase means to their own place, home. They were in Jerusalem for the Passover, so it means where they were staying in or near the city, not their homes in Galilee. Luke uses a similar phrase of Peter going home from the tomb (Luke 24:12).

decisions.choice: the disciples: the two who had gone to the tomb
decisions.reason: The article points back to Peter and the other disciple of verses 3-8.

decisions.choice: to where they were staying (B, R); the two disciples (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "to themselves" means here (meaning decision m1); Readable also says which disciples are meant (m2).

records.greek: Μαρία δὲ εἱστήκει πρὸς τῷ μνημείῳ ἔξω κλαίουσα.
records.gloss: Mary now had stood at the tomb outside weeping.

L.11: But Mary was standing outside at the tomb, weeping.

R.11: But Mary stood outside the tomb, crying.

decisions.choice: but Mary was standing: the scene turns from the two disciples to her
decisions.reason: The verb has the form of a past perfect, but with this verb it describes a lasting state: she was standing there. John does not say that she came back with the two disciples or when she arrived; he simply shows her at the tomb after they have gone.

decisions.choice: weeping: crying aloud in grief
decisions.reason: The verb is used for open mourning, as of Mary of Bethany and the mourners at Lazarus's tomb (11:31, 33). Jesus had foretold that the disciples would weep while the world rejoiced, and that their grief would turn to joy (16:20).

decisions.choice: crying
decisions.reason: The everyday word for weeping; Literal and Balanced keep "weeping".

records.greek: ὡς οὖν ἔκλαιεν παρέκυψεν εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, καὶ θεωρεῖ δύο ἀγγέλους ἐν λευκοῖς καθεζομένους, ἕνα πρὸς τῇ κεφαλῇ καὶ ἕνα πρὸς τοῖς ποσίν, ὅπου ἔκειτο τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: As therefore she was weeping she stooped into the tomb, \v 12 and sees two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where was lying the body of the Jesus.

L.11: So as she was weeping, she stooped [to look] into the tomb,
L.12: and she sees two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been lying.

R.11: While she was crying, she bent down and looked into the tomb.
R.12: She saw two angels dressed in white. They were sitting where Jesus's body had been lying, one at the head and one at the feet.

decisions.choice: two angels: messengers from God
decisions.reason: The word can mean any messenger, but here they are heavenly beings. White clothing marks such beings in the Gospels and Acts (Matthew 28:3; Mark 16:5; Acts 1:10). The two disciples saw no angels; Mary does.

decisions.choice: in white: in white clothes
decisions.reason: The adjective is plural with no noun; "clothes" is understood, a common way of speaking (Revelation 3:4-5).

decisions.choice: one at the head and one at the feet: where the body had been, with no further sign drawn
alternatives: an echo of the two cherubim over the ark
decisions.reason: Some readers have seen in the two angels a picture of the two cherubim at either end of the cover of the ark (Exodus 25:18-22). John draws no such link; the detail places the angels exactly where the body had lain.

decisions.choice: [to look] (L); stooped to look (B); bent down and looked (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to bend in order to look (see verse 5). Literal shows the supplied words in brackets.

decisions.choice: in white clothes (B); dressed in white (R)
decisions.reason: Supplies the understood "clothes" (meaning decision m2); "in white" alone is the Literal form.

records.greek: καὶ λέγουσιν αὐτῇ ἐκεῖνοι· Γύναι, τί κλαίεις;
records.gloss: And say to her those [ones], "Woman, why do you weep?"

L.13: And they say to her, "Woman, why are you weeping?"

R.13: They asked her, "Dear woman, why are you crying?"

decisions.choice: Woman: a respectful address
decisions.reason: See the note at 2:4. The address was courteous; Jesus uses it to his mother (2:4; 19:26), to the Samaritan woman (4:21), and to Mary in verse 15.

decisions.choice: why are you weeping?: a question that hints there is no cause for grief
decisions.reason: The angels do not ask for information. Their question gently suggests that weeping is out of place, since the one she mourns is not dead. Jesus asks the same question in verse 15.

decisions.choice: Woman
decisions.reason: As at 2:4 and 4:21: "Woman" on its own can sound cold, but keeping it lets readers connect the passages; the footnote says it was respectful.

decisions.choice: Dear woman
decisions.reason: For young readers "Woman" sounds rude, which the Greek is not; "Dear woman" keeps the courtesy (meaning decision m1), as at 4:21.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὅτι Ἦραν τὸν κύριόν μου, καὶ οὐκ οἶδα ποῦ ἔθηκαν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: She says to them, "They took the Lord of me, and not I know where they laid him."

L.13: She says to them, "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid Him."

R.13: She told them, "Someone has taken my Lord away, and I do not know where they put Him."

decisions.choice: my Lord: Jesus, the master she followed
alternatives: my master (a title of respect only)
decisions.reason: In verse 2 she said "the Lord"; here she says "my Lord", a more personal word of devotion. She still means his body, which she thinks someone has removed.

decisions.choice: I do not know: now singular
decisions.reason: She repeats what she said to the disciples (verse 2), but now speaks only for herself.

decisions.choice: a word that opens direct speech
decisions.reason: ὅτι here introduces her words as a quotation; it does not mean "that" or "because".

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: She speaks of Jesus, so the pronoun takes the deity_pronoun setting, as in verse 2.

decisions.choice: Someone has taken
decisions.reason: As in verse 2: Readable shows that the subject is not named.

decisions.choice: My Lord has been taken away
alternatives: They have taken my Lord away
decisions.reason: Balanced puts "my Lord" first, where her grief is, and uses the passive, since the takers are not named (meaning decision m2 at verse 2); the following "they" keeps the Greek plural.

records.greek: ταῦτα εἰποῦσα ἐστράφη εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω, καὶ θεωρεῖ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἑστῶτα, καὶ οὐκ ᾔδει ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν.
records.gloss: These things having said she turned to the [things] behind, and sees the Jesus standing, and not she knew that Jesus it is.

L.14: Having said these things, she turned around and sees Jesus standing [there], and she did not know that it was Jesus.

R.14: After saying this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there. She did not realize that it was Jesus.

decisions.choice: turned to the things behind: turned around
decisions.reason: The phrase means to turn and look back. She turns away from the tomb and the angels.

decisions.choice: she did not know that it was Jesus: she did not recognize him
decisions.reason: John does not say why. Others too fail at first to recognize the risen Jesus (Luke 24:16; John 21:4). It may have been her tears and the early light, or something changed in him; the text leaves it open. She knows him when he calls her by name (verse 16).

decisions.choice: that it was Jesus: a present tense inside reported thought
decisions.reason: Greek keeps the tense of the original thought ("it is Jesus"), where the story's past would be expected.

decisions.choice: did not realize
decisions.reason: The plain word for not recognizing someone; "know" in Literal and Balanced.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῇ Ἰησοῦς· Γύναι, τί κλαίεις;
records.gloss: Says to her Jesus, "Woman, why do you weep?"

L.15: Jesus says to her, "Woman, why are you weeping?

R.15: Jesus asked her, "Dear woman, why are you crying?

decisions.choice: Woman: a respectful address
decisions.reason: See the notes at 2:4 and verse 13. The address is courteous; Jesus uses it to his mother and to the Samaritan woman.

decisions.choice: the same question as the angels asked
decisions.reason: Jesus repeats the angels' words (verse 13). His next question follows at once, without a break in the speech.

decisions.choice: Woman
decisions.reason: As at verse 13 and 2:4: keeping "Woman" lets readers connect the passages; the footnote says it was respectful.

decisions.choice: Dear woman
decisions.reason: As at verse 13 and 4:21: "Dear woman" keeps the courtesy for young readers.

records.greek: τίνα ζητεῖς;
records.gloss: Whom do you seek?

decisions.choice: whom are you seeking?: an echo of Jesus's first words in this Gospel
alternatives: an ordinary question with no echo
decisions.reason: Jesus's first words in John are "What are you seeking?" (1:38), and he asks "Whom are you seeking?" of those who come to arrest him (18:4, 7). John may mean the reader to hear these together. The link is not certain; the question also makes plain sense on its own.

decisions.choice: whom: a person, not a thing
decisions.reason: Mary is looking for a body. Jesus asks whom she is looking for: the one she seeks is a living person.

decisions.choice: seeking (L); looking for (B, R)
decisions.reason: Everyday English at Balanced and Readable; Literal keeps "seeking", as at 1:38 and 18:4, so that the link can be seen (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἐκείνη δοκοῦσα ὅτι ὁ κηπουρός ἐστιν λέγει αὐτῷ· Κύριε, εἰ σὺ ἐβάστασας αὐτόν, εἰπέ μοι ποῦ ἔθηκας αὐτόν, κἀγὼ αὐτὸν ἀρῶ.
records.gloss: She, thinking that the gardener he is, says to him, "Sir, if you carried him, tell me where you laid him, and I him will take."
pieces: are the one who has carried

L.15: Thinking that He was the gardener, she says to Him, "Sir, if You have carried Him off, tell me where You have laid Him, and I will take Him away."

R.15: She thought He was the gardener. So she said, "Sir, if You have taken Him away, tell me where You have put Him. Then I will go and get Him."

decisions.choice: Sir: a polite address to a man she does not recognize
decisions.reason: Κύριε is the word that means Lord, but it was also the ordinary courteous way to address a man (see 4:11). Mary thinks she is speaking to the gardener, so she uses it as a polite address. A moment before she spoke of "my Lord" (verse 13).

decisions.choice: the gardener: the man who looked after the garden where the tomb was
decisions.reason: The tomb was in a garden near the place of crucifixion (19:41). Someone looking after the garden early in the morning might well have moved a body, so her guess is a natural one.

decisions.choice: if you have carried him off ... I will take him: both pronouns stressed
decisions.reason: The pronoun "you" is written out, which stresses it: she suspects this man. "I" is also stressed: she herself will take the body away. She does not stop to think how one woman could carry it.

decisions.choice: carried off: lifted and carried away
decisions.reason: ἐβάστασας means to pick up and carry. With "take" at the end of the sentence, it pictures the body being moved from place to place.

decisions.choice: Sir
decisions.reason: Mary does not know who he is, so every level has "Sir" (meaning decision m1); "Lord" would put in her mouth a recognition she has not yet made. The footnote gives "Lord", the other sense of the same Greek word.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}; {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: Mary does not recognize Jesus, but every pronoun here refers to him: the man she speaks to and the body she speaks of. All of them take the deity_pronoun setting, as when the Samaritan woman speaks to him (4:11).

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῇ Ἰησοῦς· Μαριάμ.
records.gloss: Says to her Jesus, "Mariam."

decisions.choice: Jesus calls her by name: the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name
decisions.reason: In 10:3-4 the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name", and they know his voice. Mary did not know him by sight, but she knows him when he speaks her name.

decisions.choice: Mariam: the Hebrew form of the name Mary
alternatives: a change of meaning between the two forms
decisions.reason: John writes her name in two forms: the Greek form in verses 1 and 11, and here and in verse 18 Μαριάμ, the form of the old Hebrew name Miriam. Jesus perhaps calls her by the name in the form she was used to hearing. Both forms are the same name.

decisions.choice: Mary!
decisions.reason: Every level uses the usual form of the name (meaning decision m2). The exclamation mark shows that this is a call, not a statement; the Greek has no punctuation of this kind.

records.greek: στραφεῖσα ἐκείνη λέγει αὐτῷ Ἑβραϊστί· Ραββουνι ὃ λέγεται Διδάσκαλε.
records.gloss: Having turned she says to him in Hebrew, "Rabbouni," which is said, "Teacher."

L.16: Turning, she says to Him in Hebrew, "Rabbouni!" (which means Teacher).

R.16: She turned toward Him and said in Hebrew, "Rabbouni!" (This means Teacher.)

decisions.choice: Rabbouni: "my teacher", a warm form of Rabbi, which John translates
decisions.reason: Ραββουνι is a fuller form of the title Rabbi (see 1:38), used with great respect; the blind man calls Jesus by it in Mark 10:51. As at 1:38, John translates it for readers who do not know the language. She greets him as she knew him before his death, as her teacher.

decisions.choice: in Hebrew: in the language of the Jews of the land
decisions.reason: As at 5:2 and 19:13, 17, 20, John means the local language, which in daily speech was mostly Aramaic. The form of Rabbouni is Aramaic.

decisions.choice: turning: she turns to face him fully
alternatives: she turns away from the tomb a second time
decisions.reason: She had already turned around in verse 14. John does not explain the second turning. It may be that she had turned back toward the tomb while she spoke, or that she now turns fully to him once she knows his voice.

decisions.choice: Rabbouni! (which means Teacher)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the word Mary said and John's own translation, as at 1:38 with Rabbi.

decisions.choice: turned toward him
decisions.reason: Readable shows that she turns to face Jesus (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῇ Ἰησοῦς· Μή μου ἅπτου, οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα· πορεύου δὲ πρὸς τοὺς ἀδελφούς μου καὶ εἰπὲ αὐτοῖς· Ἀναβαίνω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου καὶ πατέρα ὑμῶν καὶ θεόν μου καὶ θεὸν ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: Says to her Jesus, "Not me touch, not yet for I have ascended to the Father; go now to the brothers of me and say to them, 'I ascend to the Father of me and Father of you and God of me and God of you.'"

L.17: Jesus says to her, "Do not hold on to Me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to My brothers and sisters and say to them, 'I am ascending to My Father and your Father, and My God and your God.'"

R.17: Jesus said to her, "Do not keep holding on to Me. I have not yet gone up to the Father. But go to My brothers and sisters and tell them this: 'I am going up to My Father, who is your Father too. I am going to My God, who is your God too.'"

decisions.choice: do not hold on to me: stop clinging to me
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to touch, but also to take hold of and cling to. The command is in the present tense with "not", which most often tells someone to stop what they are already doing. Mary has taken hold of him, as the women do in Matthew 28:9, and he tells her not to keep holding him. Jesus is not forbidding any touch at all: a week later he invites Thomas to touch his wounds (20:27). The well-known rendering "Do not touch me" goes back to the older translations.

decisions.choice: for I have not yet ascended: he is not yet gone, and she need not hold him back
alternatives: she must not touch him until he has ascended and returned
she must not hold him back from ascending
decisions.reason: The reason is hard. It seems to mean that Jesus has not yet returned to the Father, so she does not need to cling to him as if he were about to vanish; there is time, and she has a message to carry. It may also mean that the old way of being with him is over: his going to the Father will bring a new kind of presence through the Spirit (14:18-19; 16:7, 22). John does not say more.

decisions.choice: my brothers: the disciples, the whole group of Jesus's followers
decisions.reason: Mary goes to "the disciples" (verse 18), so Jesus means his followers, not his brothers by birth (7:3-5). It is the first time he calls them his brothers: they now share his Father (the end of the verse; compare Matthew 28:10; Hebrews 2:11-12). The masculine plural covers a mixed group, and the followers gathered that evening (verse 19) were very likely women as well as men (compare Acts 1:14).

decisions.choice: my Father and your Father, my God and your God: a shared Father, yet named in two ways
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say "our Father". He is the Son in a way no one else is (1:14, 18), and those who believe in him become children of God through him (1:12). Through him his Father is now their Father, and his God their God (compare Ruth 1:16). The present "I am ascending" speaks of his return to the Father as already under way (13:1; 16:28).

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: The brothers are the community of disciples, men and women (meaning decision m3), so the inclusive form is the default and "brothers" the alternative.

decisions.choice: Do not hold on to me (L); Do not keep holding on to me (B, R)
decisions.reason: Shows that he is telling her to stop clinging, not forbidding a touch (meaning decision m1); the footnote gives "Do not touch me".

decisions.choice: gone up, going up (R); ascended, ascending (L, B)
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for the ascent and spells out the shared Father and God in two short sentences.

records.greek: ἔρχεται Μαριὰμ ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ ἀγγέλλουσα τοῖς μαθηταῖς ὅτι Ἑώρακα τὸν κύριον καὶ ταῦτα εἶπεν αὐτῇ.
records.gloss: Comes Mariam the Magdalene announcing to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord," and these things he said to her.

L.18: Mary Magdalene comes, announcing to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord," and [that] He had said these things to her.

R.18: So Mary Magdalene went to the disciples with the news: "I have seen the Lord!" She also told them what He had said to her.

decisions.choice: announcing: bringing news as a messenger
decisions.reason: The verb belongs to the same family as the word for messenger, or angel. Mary, sent by Jesus (verse 17), is the first to bring the news that he is risen.

decisions.choice: I have seen the Lord: the first witness to the risen Jesus
decisions.reason: The perfect tense speaks of a seeing that has lasting effect. The disciples will say the same words to Thomas (20:25). "The Lord" is now the risen Jesus.

decisions.choice: a quotation, then a report of what he said
decisions.reason: The sentence moves from her own words ("I have seen") to reported speech ("he had said these things to her"). Greek moves between the two freely.

decisions.choice: [that] (L); she reported to them what (B); She also told them what (R)
alternatives: and he said these things to her
decisions.reason: English needs a verb or a linking word for the change to reported speech (meaning decision m3). Literal shows the supplied word in brackets.

records.greek: Οὔσης οὖν ὀψίας τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ τῇ μιᾷ σαββάτων, καὶ τῶν θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων ὅπου ἦσαν οἱ μαθηταὶ διὰ τὸν φόβον τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ἦλθεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ ἔστη εἰς τὸ μέσον, καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: Being therefore evening on the day that, the first of [the] week, and the doors having been shut where were the disciples because of the fear of the Jews, came the Jesus and stood into the middle, and says to them, "Peace to you."

L.19: So when it was evening on that day, the first [day] of the week, and the doors had been shut where the disciples were, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle and says to them, "Peace to you."

R.19: It was the evening of that same Sunday, the first day of the week. The disciples were together, and they had locked the doors because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders. Then Jesus came and stood among them. He said to them, "Peace be with you."

decisions.choice: the Jews: the religious authorities in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The disciples fear the same authorities who had Jesus arrested and handed over to Pilate (18:3, 12; 19:7, 12-15), as people feared them before (7:13; 9:22; 19:38). It is not the people as a whole: the disciples themselves, and Jesus, are Jews.

decisions.choice: the evening of the same day, the first day of the week
alternatives: the start of the next day, counted from sunset
decisions.reason: "The first of the week" is the day the tomb was found empty (20:1), the day after the Sabbath. By Jewish reckoning a new day began at sunset, but John says it is still "that day": the risen Jesus meets his disciples on the day he rose.

decisions.choice: the doors had been shut and stayed shut
alternatives: the doors were being shut as he came
decisions.reason: The perfect participle describes a state: the doors were shut and remained so. John says that Jesus came and stood among them although the doors were shut (again in 20:26), but he does not say how he came in.

decisions.choice: Peace to you: the everyday greeting, now given its full weight
decisions.reason: "Peace" (shalom) was the ordinary Jewish greeting, a wish for wholeness and well-being from God. On Jesus's lips after his death and rising it is more than a greeting: it is the peace he promised to leave them (14:27; 16:33), now given.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: historic present at Literal ("says", "comes"); past tense at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in John, Literal keeps John's present tense ("says" in 20:19, 22, 27, 29; "comes" in 20:26), which makes the story vivid; Balanced and Readable use the past, as English tells a story. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: behind locked doors (B); locked, were together (R); Peace to you (L, B); Peace be with you (R)
decisions.reason: Doors shut out of fear were barred or bolted, so Balanced and Readable say "locked"; Literal keeps "shut". "Where the disciples were" implies they were in one place, which Balanced says with "behind locked doors" and Readable with "together". Readable uses the fuller form of the greeting that English speakers know; every level keeps "peace".

records.heading: Jesus appears to the disciples

records.greek: καὶ τοῦτο εἰπὼν ἔδειξεν τὰς χεῖρας καὶ τὴν πλευρὰν αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: And this having said he showed the hands and the side to them.

L.20: And having said this, He showed them [His] hands and [His] side.

R.20: After saying this, He showed them the wounds in His hands and His side.

decisions.choice: the hands and side: the wounds of the cross, showing the risen one is the one crucified
alternatives: a proof only that he had a body
decisions.reason: His hands bore the marks of the nails (20:25) and his side the wound of the soldier's spear (19:34). By showing them, Jesus makes himself known: the one who stands among them is the same one who died. The wounds remain in his risen body (20:27).

decisions.choice: side: the side of the chest, where the spear went in
decisions.reason: The word is the one used in 19:34 of the spear wound, from which blood and water came out. Only John tells of it; in Luke 24:39-40 Jesus shows his hands and feet.

decisions.choice: [his] hands and [his] side (L); the wounds in his hands and his side (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says "the hands and the side"; English needs "his", which Literal brackets. Readable names the wounds, which is what he showed (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἐχάρησαν οὖν οἱ μαθηταὶ ἰδόντες τὸν κύριον.
records.gloss: Rejoiced therefore the disciples having seen the Lord.

L.20: So the disciples rejoiced, having seen the Lord.

R.20: The disciples were full of joy when they saw the Lord.

decisions.choice: the joy Jesus promised: "I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice"
decisions.reason: In 16:20-22 Jesus told them that their grief would turn to joy when they saw him again, and that no one would take that joy from them. John uses the same verb for rejoice here: the promise is kept.

decisions.choice: the Lord: Jesus, now known as the risen Lord
alternatives: sir or master, an address of respect
decisions.reason: The narrator calls Jesus "the Lord" here, as Mary Magdalene has just done (20:18, "I have seen the Lord") and the disciples will say to Thomas (20:25). The title points toward Thomas's confession, "My Lord and my God" (20:28).

decisions.choice: they rejoiced because they saw him
alternatives: they rejoiced, and also saw him
decisions.reason: The word "therefore" and the participle "having seen" tie the joy to the sight: they rejoiced when, and because, they saw the Lord.

decisions.choice: were full of joy
decisions.reason: Readable uses the noun "joy", the plainer expression, which also keeps the link with Jesus's promise of joy in 16:20-22.

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς πάλιν· Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν· καθὼς ἀπέσταλκέν με ὁ πατήρ, κἀγὼ πέμπω ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: Said therefore to them the Jesus again, "Peace to you; just as has sent me the Father, I also send you."

L.21: So Jesus said to them again, "Peace to you. Just as the Father has sent Me, I also send you."

R.21: Again Jesus said to them, "Peace be with you. The Father has sent Me. In the same way, I am sending you."

decisions.choice: has sent, send: two Greek verbs with the same meaning here
alternatives: a difference in meaning between the two verbs, such as an official commission for the first
decisions.reason: John uses both verbs, ἀπέσταλκέν and πέμπω, of the Father sending the Son (for example 3:17 and 5:23-24), and both of Jesus sending others (4:38; 13:20). Here they most likely vary for style, and the point is that the sendings match. Because the first verb is related to the word "apostle", some take it to stress an official commission, but John uses the two freely.

decisions.choice: the Father has sent: a sending that still stands; I send: now
decisions.reason: The first verb is perfect: the Father sent Jesus and he remains the one sent. The second is present: Jesus is sending them now, as he said he would in his prayer (17:18).

decisions.choice: the disciples' mission is patterned on Jesus's own
alternatives: a separate mission of their own
decisions.reason: Jesus is "the one sent" throughout John (3:17; 5:36; 17:3, 8). Now the disciples share his mission in the world, as 13:20 and 17:18 foretold. What follows, the gift of the Spirit and the word about forgiving sins (20:22-23), belongs to this sending.

decisions.choice: Peace to you again: a second greeting that opens the commissioning
decisions.reason: Jesus has already greeted them (20:19). Saying it again marks a new start: having shown them his wounds, he now sends them out, and he sends them with his peace (14:27).

decisions.choice: In the way that ... I am sending you (B); The Father has sent me. In the same way, I am sending you. (R)
alternatives: As the Father has sent me, so I send you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out that the two sendings match (meaning decision m3), with wording like 17:18; the English present "am sending" fits a sending that happens now (m2). Readable keeps "Peace be with you" as in 20:19.

records.greek: καὶ τοῦτο εἰπὼν ἐνεφύσησεν καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Λάβετε πνεῦμα ἅγιον·
records.gloss: And this having said he breathed on and says to them, "Receive Holy Spirit."

L.22: And having said this, He breathed on [them] and says to them, "Receive [the] Holy Spirit."

R.22: Then He breathed on them. He said, "Receive the Holy Spirit."

decisions.choice: he breathed on them: echoing God breathing life into the first man
alternatives: an ordinary gesture with no echo intended
decisions.reason: The verb ἐνεφύσησεν is rare. The same form is used in the Greek Old Testament of God breathing the breath of life into the man he had formed (Genesis 2:7), and the verb is used when the breath of God gives life to the dead bones (Ezekiel 37:9). The echo suggests a new creation: the risen Jesus gives new life by his Spirit (compare 3:5-8). The text does not say this in so many words.

decisions.choice: Receive the Holy Spirit: Jesus gives the Spirit he promised, now that he is glorified
alternatives: only a promise of a later gift
a different gift from the Spirit poured out at Pentecost
decisions.reason: Jesus had said that the Spirit would be given once he was glorified (7:39) and that he would send the Advocate when he went away (14:16-17, 26; 15:26; 16:7). Here he gives the Spirit with a word and a gesture. John does not say how this relates to the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:1-4). It may be John's account of the same gift, a first giving followed by a fuller one, or a sign of what was to come; the text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: Holy Spirit without the article: God's Spirit, not a mere influence
alternatives: a gift or power of the Spirit, as distinct from the Spirit himself
decisions.reason: Greek often leaves out the article with "Holy Spirit" (as in 1:33). Some take the lack of the article to mean a gift from the Spirit, but in this setting, after the promises of chapters 14-16, it is the Holy Spirit himself who is given. So the word has a capital S.

decisions.choice: breathed on [them]; Receive [the] Holy Spirit (L); them, the (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek verb has no object, but those he breathed on are the disciples he is speaking to. English needs "the" before "Holy Spirit" (meaning decision m3). Literal brackets both.

records.greek: ἄν τινων ἀφῆτε τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀφέωνται αὐτοῖς· ἄν τινων κρατῆτε κεκράτηνται.
records.gloss: If of any you forgive the sins, they have been forgiven to them; if of any you retain, they have been retained.

L.23: If you forgive the sins of any, they have been forgiven them; if you retain [the sins] of any, they have been retained.

R.23: When you forgive people's sins, those sins are forgiven. When you hold people's sins against them, those sins remain.

decisions.choice: an authority given to the disciples as a community sent by Jesus
alternatives: an authority given to particular leaders only
a power to forgive apart from God
decisions.reason: The verbs are plural: Jesus speaks to the disciples gathered in the room (20:19), who are sent as he was sent and have received the Spirit (20:21-22). The forgiving of sins belongs to that mission. The text does not say how it is to be carried out. Later churches applied it in different ways: some to the forgiveness pronounced by ordained ministers, others to the preaching of the gospel and the discipline of the whole church. The words themselves do not decide between these.

decisions.choice: they have been forgiven, they have been retained: a result that stands, with God as the one who forgives
alternatives: the disciples forgive in their own right
decisions.reason: Both verbs are perfect passives. The passive leaves the one who forgives unnamed; in the Bible only God forgives sins in the end (Mark 2:7). The perfect says the result stands. Whether it means that God has already forgiven what they declare forgiven, or that he confirms what they do, is debated; the tense alone does not settle it.

decisions.choice: forgive and retain: release and hold fast
decisions.reason: The verb for "forgive" means to let go or release; the verb for "retain", κρατῆτε, means to hold on to or keep hold of. Sins are either released from people or kept bound to them. Compare "bind" and "loose" in Matthew 16:19 and 18:18.

decisions.choice: Whose sins ... they stand forgiven ... stand retained (B); hold people's sins against them ... remain (R)
alternatives: they are forgiven ... they are retained
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "stand" for the perfect tense, a result that holds (meaning decision m2). Readable puts "retain" into plain words, holding a wrong against someone, and says the sins remain, which is the opposite of forgiven (m3). "People" and "whose" include men and women.

records.greek: Θωμᾶς δὲ εἷς ἐκ τῶν δώδεκα, ὁ λεγόμενος Δίδυμος, οὐκ ἦν μετ’ αὐτῶν ὅτε ἦλθεν Ἰησοῦς.
records.gloss: Thomas but, one of the Twelve, the [one] called Didymus, not was with them when came Jesus.

L.24: But Thomas, one of the Twelve, the [one] called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.

R.24: But Thomas was not with them when Jesus came. He was one of the twelve disciples, and he was called the Twin.

decisions.choice: Thomas called Didymus: both names mean "twin"
decisions.reason: As in 11:16, John gives the Greek word for Thomas's Semitic name, which means "twin". Whose twin he was is never said.

decisions.choice: the Twelve: the inner group Jesus chose
decisions.reason: "The Twelve" are the disciples Jesus chose (6:67-71). John notes that Thomas belongs to them, so his absence leaves one of the chosen witnesses without the experience the others had. The group in 20:19 is called simply "the disciples" and may have included others besides the Twelve.

decisions.choice: Didymus (which means Twin) (B); the twelve disciples, the Twin (R)
decisions.reason: As at 11:16, Balanced adds the meaning of the name and Readable gives only the meaning. Readable says "the twelve disciples" for the title "the Twelve" and splits the sentence.

records.greek: ἔλεγον οὖν αὐτῷ οἱ ἄλλοι μαθηταί· Ἑωράκαμεν τὸν κύριον.
records.gloss: Were saying therefore to him the other disciples, "We have seen the Lord."

L.25: So the other disciples were saying to him, "We have seen the Lord."

R.25: The other disciples told him again and again, "We have seen the Lord!"

decisions.choice: were saying: telling him more than once
decisions.reason: The verb is imperfect, which can describe an action repeated or kept up. They went on telling him, and he went on refusing.

decisions.choice: We have seen the Lord: the same witness Mary Magdalene gave
decisions.reason: Mary told the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" (20:18), with the same verb in the same tense. Now the disciples give that witness to Thomas. The perfect tense speaks of a seeing whose effect lasts.

decisions.choice: kept telling (B); told him again and again (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the repeated telling (meaning decision m1). The exclamation mark shows their excitement, which the setting implies.

records.greek: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Ἐὰν μὴ ἴδω ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτοῦ τὸν τύπον τῶν ἥλων καὶ βάλω τὸν δάκτυλόν μου εἰς τὸν τύπον τῶν ἥλων καὶ βάλω μου τὴν χεῖρα εἰς τὴν πλευρὰν αὐτοῦ, οὐ μὴ πιστεύσω.
records.gloss: He but said to them, "If not I see in the hands of him the imprint of the nails and put the finger of me into the imprint of the nails and put of me the hand into the side of him, not not I will believe."

L.25: But he said to them, "If I do not see in His hands the imprint of the nails, and put my finger into the imprint of the nails, and put my hand into His side, I will certainly not believe."

R.25: But Thomas said, "First I must see the marks of the nails in His hands. I must put my finger into those marks and put my hand into His side. If I do not, I will never believe."

decisions.choice: I will certainly not believe: the strongest denial in Greek
alternatives: I will not believe (a plain refusal)
decisions.reason: Two negatives together, "not" and "not", make the firmest possible denial. Thomas asks to see what the others saw (20:20) and to touch it as well.

decisions.choice: imprint: the mark left by the nails
decisions.reason: The word means the mark struck or pressed into something, such as the impression of a seal. Here it is the wound the nails left.

decisions.choice: nails: Jesus was nailed to the cross
decisions.reason: The Romans sometimes tied a condemned person to the cross and sometimes nailed them. This is the only place in the Gospels that mentions nails in Jesus's crucifixion (compare Luke 24:39; Colossians 2:14). The word for "hand" can include the wrist.

decisions.choice: I will never believe it unless ... (B); First I must ... If I do not, I will never believe. (R)
alternatives: Unless I see ..., I will never believe (Greek order)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the refusal first, which is natural English for a long condition; Readable breaks the conditions into short sentences and names Thomas as the speaker. Literal keeps the Greek order.

records.greek: Καὶ μεθ’ ἡμέρας ὀκτὼ πάλιν ἦσαν ἔσω οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ Θωμᾶς μετ’ αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: And after days eight again were inside the disciples of him and Thomas with them.

L.26: And after eight days His disciples were again inside, and Thomas [was] with them.

R.26: A week later, on the next Sunday, Jesus's disciples were together inside again. This time Thomas was with them.

decisions.choice: after eight days: a week later, on the next first day of the week
decisions.reason: Days were counted inclusively, so the first day and the last are both counted. "After eight days" means the same day the next week, that is, again the first day of the week (20:19).

decisions.choice: again inside: in the same place as before
decisions.reason: "Again" and "inside" point back to the scene of 20:19: the disciples are gathered behind shut doors once more. The difference is that Thomas is now there.

decisions.choice: A week later (B, R); on the next Sunday (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom (meaning decision m1). Readable names the day as in 20:19 and names Jesus, whom the Greek refers to as "his".

records.heading: Jesus and Thomas

records.greek: ἔρχεται ὁ Ἰησοῦς τῶν θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων, καὶ ἔστη εἰς τὸ μέσον καὶ εἶπεν· Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: Comes the Jesus, the doors having been shut, and stood into the middle and said, "Peace to you."

L.26: Jesus comes, the doors having been shut, and stood in the middle and said, "Peace to you."

R.26: The doors were locked, but Jesus came and stood among them. He said, "Peace be with you."

decisions.choice: the doors having been shut: though the doors were shut
alternatives: after the doors had been shut, simply giving the time
decisions.reason: The phrase stands on its own beside the verb, and the context gives it the sense "although": the shut doors did not keep him out. As in 20:19, John does not say how he came in.

decisions.choice: Peace to you: the same greeting a third time
decisions.reason: Jesus greets them exactly as he did a week before (20:19, 21). The greeting carries the peace he promised (14:27), now offered to Thomas too.

decisions.choice: Though the doors were locked, Jesus came (B); The doors were locked, but (R)
alternatives: Jesus comes, the doors having been shut (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the sense "although" (meaning decision m1) and use the past tense (see 20:19 on the historic present). "Locked" and "Peace be with you" as in 20:19.

records.greek: εἶτα λέγει τῷ Θωμᾷ· Φέρε τὸν δάκτυλόν σου ὧδε καὶ ἴδε τὰς χεῖράς μου, καὶ φέρε τὴν χεῖρά σου καὶ βάλε εἰς τὴν πλευράν μου, καὶ μὴ γίνου ἄπιστος ἀλλὰ πιστός.
records.gloss: Then he says to the Thomas, "Bring the finger of you here and see the hands of me, and bring the hand of you and put into the side of me, and not become unbelieving but believing."

L.27: Then He says to Thomas, "Bring your finger here and see My hands, and bring your hand and put [it] into My side, and do not be unbelieving, but believing."

R.27: Then He said to Thomas, "Here, put your finger on My hands and look at them. Stretch out your hand and put it into My side. Do not refuse to believe any longer. Believe!"

decisions.choice: Jesus answers Thomas's demand point by point
decisions.reason: Thomas had named his finger, the hands, his hand and the side (20:25). Jesus offers each of these, though he was not there when Thomas spoke. He knows what is in people (1:47-48; 2:25). The text does not say that Thomas then touched him.

decisions.choice: unbelieving, believing: not believing and believing
alternatives: faithless and faithful, that is, disloyal and loyal
decisions.reason: The two words, ἄπιστος and πιστός, can mean "unfaithful" and "faithful". Here they belong to the same word family as "believe", and the context is about believing (20:25, 29, 31), so they mean refusing to believe and believing.

decisions.choice: do not be, do not become: do not go on as one who refuses to believe
decisions.reason: The verb means "become" or "be", in a present-tense command with "not". Jesus calls Thomas at the point of choosing not to settle into unbelief but to believe.

decisions.choice: Put your finger here (B); put your finger on my hands, Stretch out your hand (R); Do not be unbelieving any longer, but believing (B); Do not refuse to believe any longer. Believe! (R)
alternatives: Bring your finger here; Stop doubting
decisions.reason: The verb "bring" here means to move a hand or finger toward something; Balanced says "put" for the finger and keeps "bring" for the hand, and Readable says "put" and "stretch out" and joins the finger to the hands it is to touch. Balanced and Readable keep the word family of "believe" (meaning decision m2) rather than "doubt", and "any longer" carries the sense of m3.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη Θωμᾶς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου.
records.gloss: Answered Thomas and said to him, "The Lord of me and the God of me."

L.28: Thomas answered and said to Him, "My Lord and my God!"

R.28: Thomas said to Him, "My Lord and my God!"

decisions.choice: My Lord and my God: Thomas confesses Jesus himself as Lord and God
alternatives: an exclamation of surprise addressed to God the Father
decisions.reason: Thomas "said to him": the words are spoken to Jesus. They are the highest confession in the Gospel and close the frame John opened at the start, "the Word was God" (1:1) and "the one and only God" who makes the Father known (1:18). The book that began by saying who the Word is ends with a disciple saying it to his face.

decisions.choice: the nominative with the article used as an address
alternatives: a statement: "(he is) my Lord and my God"
decisions.reason: Greek often uses the nominative with the article to address someone (for example Mark 14:36, "Abba, Father"). With "said to him", the words are a cry addressed to Jesus.

decisions.choice: Lord and God: the way Israel addressed its God
decisions.reason: The Psalms join the two words in calling on the God of Israel: "my God and my Lord" (Psalm 35:23). Thomas gives Jesus the names Israel gave to God.

decisions.choice: my: a personal confession
decisions.reason: Thomas does not only say who Jesus is; he says whose he is: "my" Lord, "my" God.

decisions.choice: My Lord and my God!
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the exact words, the climax of the book's confession. "My" is Thomas speaking of himself, so it takes no reader setting; "him" refers to Jesus and does.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ὅτι ἑώρακάς με πεπίστευκας;
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, "Because you have seen me, you have believed?"

L.29: Jesus says to him, "Because you have seen Me, you have believed?

R.29: Jesus said to him, "Is it because you have seen Me that you believe?

decisions.choice: a question (SBLGNT)
alternatives: a statement: "Because you have seen me, you have believed."
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts have no punctuation, and the words can be read either way. The SBLGNT prints a question. Either way Jesus accepts Thomas's belief and points beyond it to those who will believe without seeing.

decisions.choice: you have seen, you have believed: a sight that brought lasting belief
decisions.reason: Both verbs are perfect: Thomas has seen, and as a result he now believes.

decisions.choice: Have you believed because ...? (B); Is it because ... that you believe? (R)
alternatives: Because you have seen me, you have believed? (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use English question order (meaning decision m1). Readable says "believe", the state that "have believed" describes (m2).

records.greek: μακάριοι οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες καὶ πιστεύσαντες.
records.gloss: Blessed the [ones] not having seen and having believed.

L.29: Blessed [are] those who did not see and [yet] believed."

R.29: God's blessing is on those who have not seen Me and still believe."

decisions.choice: blessed: in a good state in God's sight
decisions.reason: The word is the one in 13:17, the only other place John uses it, and in the beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-11). It declares people well off before God, whatever they feel.

decisions.choice: those who did not see and believed: those who come to believe without seeing
alternatives: the disciples, who believed before they saw
decisions.reason: The participles are aorist and describe the whole group of those who believe without seeing. They are those Jesus prayed for, who believe through the disciples' word (17:20), and the readers John writes for in the next verses (20:31). Jesus does not take back his acceptance of Thomas's belief.

decisions.choice: and: and yet
decisions.reason: The word "and" joins two things that do not usually go together, not seeing and believing, so it has the force "and yet".

decisions.choice: Blessed are those who have believed without having seen (B); God's blessing is on those who have not seen me and still believe (R)
alternatives: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "blessed" as at 13:17; Readable names God as the one who blesses, as it does there. Balanced and Readable express "and yet" (meaning decision m3) in natural English, and Readable supplies "me", whom they have not seen.

records.greek: Πολλὰ μὲν οὖν καὶ ἄλλα σημεῖα ἐποίησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐνώπιον τῶν μαθητῶν, ἃ οὐκ ἔστιν γεγραμμένα ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τούτῳ·
records.gloss: Many indeed therefore also other signs did the Jesus before the disciples, which not are written in the book this.

L.30: So then, Jesus also did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book.

R.30: Jesus did many other signs while his disciples were watching. They are not written in this book.

decisions.choice: signs: deeds that point to who Jesus is
decisions.reason: "Signs" is John's word for the deeds of Jesus that show his glory and lead people to believe (2:11; 12:37). John has told a selection of them; there were many more (21:25).

decisions.choice: So then ... but these: a contrast with the next sentence
decisions.reason: The opening words prepare for the contrast in 20:31: many signs are not written, but these are written for a purpose. The sentence looks back over the whole book.

decisions.choice: in the presence of the disciples: done before witnesses
decisions.reason: The disciples saw the signs and can testify to them, because they have been with Jesus from the beginning (15:27). The book rests on their witness (19:35; 21:24).

decisions.choice: while the disciples looked on (B); while his disciples were watching (R); written down (B)
alternatives: in the presence of the disciples
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the phrase into everyday words that keep the idea of witnesses (meaning decision m3). Readable says "his disciples" and makes two sentences.

records.heading: Why this book was written

records.greek: ταῦτα δὲ γέγραπται ἵνα πιστεύητε ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν ὁ χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ ἵνα πιστεύοντες ζωὴν ἔχητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: These but have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the God, and so that believing life you may have in the name of him.

L.31: But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have life in His name.

R.31: But these signs are written down so that you will believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. And when you believe, you will have life through Him.

decisions.choice: so that you may believe, present tense (SBLGNT)
alternatives: πιστεύσητε, aorist: "so that you may come to believe"
decisions.reason: Some of the oldest manuscripts, including Codex Vaticanus and the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, and probably the papyrus P66, have the present tense, which can mean "continue to believe". Many others, including Codex Alexandrinus and most later manuscripts, have the aorist, which can mean "come to believe". The difference bears on whether the book was written mainly to strengthen believers or to bring others to believe. Yet tenses in purpose clauses like this do not draw a sharp line, and John uses both for both purposes (compare 19:35; 11:15), so the book can serve both. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Christ, the Son of God: a title, the Messiah, with its fullest meaning
decisions.reason: "The Christ" is the anointed king Israel was waiting for (1:41; 4:25-26; 7:41-42). Martha confessed Jesus in the same words: "you are the Christ, the Son of God" (11:27). John fills "Son of God" with the meaning the whole book has given it (1:18; 5:18; 10:30-36; 20:28).

decisions.choice: life: eternal life, the life of God given now
decisions.reason: "Life" here is the eternal life John speaks of throughout (3:15-16; 5:24; 10:10; 17:3): life with God that begins when a person believes and does not end.

decisions.choice: in his name: through him, through who he is
decisions.reason: A name stands for the person. Life "in his name" is life that comes through Jesus and belongs to those joined to him, as "believe in his name" means to believe in him (1:12; 3:18).

decisions.choice: these: the signs written in this book
decisions.reason: "These" picks up the signs of 20:30 that are written, in contrast to the many that are not. The book as a whole was written for this purpose.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: "The Christ" is a title here, so every level writes "the" before it (see the book's terms); the reader may choose "Messiah".

decisions.choice: by believing have life (B); these signs; And when you believe, you will have life through him (R)
alternatives: believing, you may have life in his name (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced renders the participle "by believing", which keeps the link between believing and having life. Readable names "these" as the signs (meaning decision m5) and says "through him" for "in his name" (m4). "You may believe" is kept at Balanced so that the meaning of the tense stays as open as the Greek (m1).
